words.definition: The quality of being open to more than one interpretation.
words.example: The ambiguity of her reply left us unsure whether she had agreed or refused.
words.mnemonic: 'ambi-' means both (as in ambidextrous) — a meaning pulling in both directions at once.

words.definition: Sticking or fitting together to form a united, well-connected whole.
words.example: The coach turned a group of strangers into a cohesive team that moved as one.
words.mnemonic: 'co-' (together) + '-hes-' (stick, as in adhesive): things firmly stuck together.

words.definition: Going on at length while wandering from topic to topic without a clear point.
words.example: His rambling speech drifted from taxes to his childhood dog before anyone could follow it.
words.mnemonic: Picture someone on a country ramble — wandering off with no destination in mind.

words.definition: Clear enough to let light pass so objects behind can be seen plainly.
words.example: The aquarium's transparent walls let visitors watch the sharks glide past.
words.mnemonic: 'trans-' (through) + '-parent' (appear): what's behind it appears right through.

words.definition: Letting some light pass through while blurring whatever lies behind.
words.example: The frosted, translucent glass in the bathroom door let in daylight but hid any shapes.
words.mnemonic: 'trans-' (through) + 'lucent' (shining): light shines through, but images don't — halfway between clear and solid.

words.definition: Written or printed clearly enough to be read with ease.
words.example: Her handwriting was so legible that even the pharmacist read the note without squinting.
words.mnemonic: 'leg-' comes from Latin 'legere,' to read (as in lecture, legend): if it's legible, you can read it.

words.definition: Clear enough for the mind to grasp; able to be understood.
words.example: Over the crackling phone line, only a few intelligible words reached her.
words.mnemonic: Shares a root with 'intelligent' — an intelligent mind can grasp it.

words.definition: So unclear that it cannot be understood at all.
words.example: The toddler's excited, unintelligible chatter meant nothing to the visitors.
words.mnemonic: 'un-' (not) + intelligible: the opposite of what even an intelligent listener could grasp.

words.definition: Able to be grasped by the mind without difficulty.
words.example: The professor rephrased the theory until it was comprehensible to first-year students.
words.mnemonic: Think of 'comprehend' — if you can comprehend it, it is this.

words.definition: To make someone lose their sense of direction or bearings.
words.example: The identical hallways of the hospital disoriented every new patient.
words.mnemonic: 'dis-' (undo) + 'orient' (find your east/bearings): to un-orient someone.

words.definition: To upset someone's calm so they become nervous and confused.
words.example: The sudden question flustered the witness, who fumbled and dropped his notes.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'flurry' + 'bluster' — a sudden flurry of nerves.

words.definition: To baffle someone so thoroughly they cannot respond.
words.example: The riddle flummoxed even the cleverest students in the class.
words.mnemonic: The goofy sound 'flummox' — imagine being so baffled all you can stammer is 'flum...?'

words.definition: To shock or astonish someone so much they can barely think.
words.example: The size of the lottery win stupefied him; he sat speechless for an hour.
words.mnemonic: Shares a root with 'stupid' and 'stupor' — stunned into a helpless stupor.

words.definition: To muddle the mind so it cannot think clearly.
words.example: The heat and lack of sleep addled her so badly she forgot her own address.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'muddle' — an addled brain is a muddled brain (also an 'addled egg' is a spoiled one).

words.definition: To stun someone so they briefly cannot think or see clearly.
words.example: The bright stage lights dazed the singer for a moment as she stepped out.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'days' — so stunned you lose track of your days.

words.definition: To make something look hazy, smeared, or hard to see clearly.
words.example: Tears began to blur her view of the finish line.
words.mnemonic: "Blur" sounds like "brr" — shivering shakes everything into a fuzzy smear.

words.definition: To make something easier to understand or do by removing difficulty.
words.example: The teacher tried to simplify the equation for her confused students.
words.mnemonic: "Simple" + "-ify" literally means "to make simple."

words.definition: To extract the purest or most essential part of something.
words.example: She managed to distill her hour-long lecture into three key points.
words.mnemonic: A whiskey still drips liquid drop by drop, keeping only the pure essence.

words.definition: So clear that light passes right through or meaning is instantly grasped.
words.example: The pellucid mountain stream let us count every pebble on its bed.
words.mnemonic: Hear "lucid" (clear) hiding inside pel-LUCID — clear, then extra clear.

words.definition: Completely clear and transparent, or easy to understand and free of confusion.
words.example: We could see every pebble at the bottom of the limpid mountain stream.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'limp' + 'lipid' — picture a still pool so clear it looks like liquid glass, no ripples to cloud it.

words.definition: Producing strong, bright, lifelike images in the mind or eye.
words.example: Her vivid description made me feel like I was standing in ancient Rome.
words.mnemonic: "Vivid" shares "viv" with "revive" and "alive" — vivid things feel alive.

words.definition: Able to be touched, or clearly real rather than abstract.
words.example: After months of planning, the profits were finally tangible.
words.mnemonic: From Latin "tangere," to touch — the same root as "tango," where partners touch.

words.definition: So intense or obvious that it can almost be physically felt.
words.example: The tension in the courtroom was palpable as the verdict drew near.
words.mnemonic: A doctor "palpates" by feeling with the palms — palpable means feelable.

words.definition: Plainly obvious and easily seen or understood.
words.example: His manifest joy at the reunion brought everyone to tears.
words.mnemonic: "Man" + "fest" — at a festival everything is out in the open for all to see.

words.definition: Easily seen or understood, leaving no room for doubt.
words.example: It was evident from her packed bags that she was leaving for good.
words.mnemonic: "Evident" holds "evidence" — evidence is what makes something plain to all.

words.definition: Clearly visible or easily understood at first glance.
words.example: The damage became apparent only after we turned on the lights.
words.mnemonic: "Apparent" starts with "appear" — what appears is apparent.

words.definition: Standing out so as to be easily noticed or widely known.
words.example: A prominent scar ran across the old boxer's cheek.
words.mnemonic: "Prominent" is kin to "promontory," a cliff that juts out — both stick out.

words.definition: Able to be noticed or sensed, though sometimes only slightly.
words.example: There was a perceptible drop in temperature as we entered the cave.
words.mnemonic: "Perceive" + "-ible" — able to be perceived.

words.definition: Too small or gradual to be noticed or sensed.
words.example: The clock's hands crept forward at an imperceptible pace.
words.mnemonic: The prefix "im-" means "not" — so it is simply "not perceivable."

words.definition: To wander or follow a winding, aimless course.
words.example: We let the afternoon slip by, meandering through the old town's alleys.
words.mnemonic: The Menderes River in Turkey (ancient "Maeander") twists so wildly it named the word.

words.definition: To wander away from the main topic when speaking or writing.
words.example: Halfway through the lecture, the professor began to digress into stories about his college days.
words.mnemonic: Break it into di- (away) + -gress (to step): you step away from the point.

words.definition: A sudden shift onto an unrelated subject or line of thinking.
words.example: She went off on a tangent about her cat right in the middle of the budget meeting.
words.mnemonic: In geometry a tangent line touches a circle then shoots off in its own direction — just like a stray thought.

words.definition: Lacking smooth or logical connection between its parts.
words.example: His disjointed explanation jumped from one idea to another with no clear link.
words.mnemonic: DIS + JOINT: the joints are undone, so the pieces no longer hold together.

words.definition: Distorted or mixed up so that the meaning is hard to grasp.
words.example: The radio message came through so garbled that we couldn't make out a single word.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'gargled' — words gargled in your throat come out messy and unclear.

words.definition: A confused, disordered mixture of things thrown together.
words.example: Her desk was a jumble of papers, pens, and half-eaten snacks.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'tumble' — imagine socks tumbling in a dryer into one messy heap.

words.definition: To mix or throw things together in a hurried, disordered way.
words.example: He scrambled the puzzle pieces so no one could tell what the picture was.
words.mnemonic: Think scrambled eggs — beaten and stirred until nothing keeps its original shape.

words.definition: A twisted, knotted mass that is hard to separate.
words.example: The kitten turned the ball of yarn into a hopeless tangle.
words.mnemonic: Picture the 'dangle' of cords behind a TV, all twisted around each other.

words.definition: Complicated and difficult to solve or understand.
words.example: The lawyers spent weeks untangling the knotty legal question.
words.mnemonic: Full of knots — a rope covered in knots is hard to work with, and so is such a problem.

words.definition: Extremely complicated, with many confusing twists and passages.
words.example: Navigating the labyrinthine bureaucracy took months of forms and phone calls.
words.mnemonic: From 'labyrinth,' the maze that trapped the Minotaur — full of bewildering twisting passages.

words.definition: Full of many twists, turns, or complications.
words.example: The mountain road was so tortuous that passengers felt carsick within minutes.
words.mnemonic: Shares a root with 'torque' (to twist); the path twists again and again. Don't confuse it with 'torturous.'

words.definition: Taking a long, roundabout route rather than a direct one.
words.example: He took a circuitous route home to avoid the highway traffic.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'circuit' inside — a circuit loops all the way around instead of going straight.

words.definition: The use of too many words, or needlessly wordy language.
words.example: The contract's dense verbiage buried the one clause that actually mattered.
words.mnemonic: 'Verb' + '-iage' — a pile of words heaped up like extra baggage.

words.definition: Using far too many words and therefore tedious.
words.example: The professor's prolix answers turned a simple question into an hour-long ordeal.
words.mnemonic: Starts like 'prolong' — such speech prolongs itself with endless extra words.

words.definition: Easy to understand or do; simple and direct.
words.example: The instructions were straightforward, so we assembled the shelf in ten minutes.
words.mnemonic: Straight + forward — going straight ahead, with no twists or detours.

words.definition: Openness and honesty that lets others clearly see what is happening.
words.example: Voters demanded greater transparency about how the campaign spent its money.
words.mnemonic: Think of a clear glass window you can see straight through — nothing is hidden.

words.definition: The quality of being hard to see through, or difficult to understand.
words.example: The frosted glass had enough opacity to hide the room's contents from the street.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'a-PASS-ity' — light can't pass through it.

words.definition: Showing sharp insight or the ability to see deeply into things.
words.example: The detective's penetrating questions made the suspect stumble over his story.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'penetrare,' to pierce through — like an X-ray that goes right past the surface.

words.definition: Keen skill and quickness in judgment or understanding.
words.example: Her business acumen turned a failing corner shop into a national chain.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'acus' (needle) — a sharp needle-point of the mind that catches every cue.

words.definition: Having keen mental sharpness and a quick grasp of situations.
words.example: The perspicacious teacher spotted the cheating long before anyone else suspected it.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'per-SPEC-acious' — picture someone in spectacles (specs) who sees everything clearly.

words.definition: Showing clever judgment and practical cunning, especially about people or money.
words.example: A shrewd investor, she sold every share a week before the crash.
words.mnemonic: 'Shrewd' hides 'shrew' — a tiny, quick animal that outwits creatures far bigger than itself.

words.definition: Keeping careful watch for possible danger or trouble.
words.example: The vigilant lifeguard spotted the struggling swimmer within seconds.
words.mnemonic: Think 'vigil' — someone who stays awake all night to keep watch is vigilant.

words.definition: Carefully watching or listening and noticing small details.
words.example: The attentive waiter refilled our glasses before we even had to ask.
words.mnemonic: Picture 'at-TENT-ive' — a soldier in a tent, ears pricked to every sound outside.

words.definition: Not aware of what is happening around you.
words.example: Lost in his music, he was oblivious to the train pulling away without him.
words.mnemonic: Cousin of 'oblivion' — fall into oblivion and you forget and notice nothing.

words.definition: Paying no attention to danger, warnings, or consequences.
words.example: Heedless of the thin-ice signs, the boys sprinted onto the frozen lake.
words.mnemonic: 'Heed' means to pay attention; the '-less' strips it clean away.

words.definition: Unable to concentrate because your mind is pulled elsewhere.
words.example: Distracted by his buzzing phone, the driver drifted into the next lane.
words.mnemonic: 'Dis-tract' — Latin 'tractus,' to pull; your focus is dragged apart in different directions.

words.definition: So absorbed in your own thoughts that you barely notice others.
words.example: Preoccupied with tomorrow's exam, she barely touched her dinner.
words.mnemonic: 'Pre-occupied' — the seats of your mind are taken in advance, so nothing new can sit down.

words.definition: A messy, difficult situation hard to escape; also soft, muddy ground.
words.example: The lawsuit dragged the company into a financial quagmire that lasted years.
words.mnemonic: 'Quag' + 'mire' — ground that quakes like jelly and mires you in mud.

words.definition: A confusing tangle of things, or a stretch of soft, wet ground.
words.example: New hires drown in a morass of forms, logins, and passwords on their first day.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'more-mass' — an ever-growing swampy mass that bogs you down.

words.definition: Deep mud, or a troublesome situation that traps you.
words.example: The truck's wheels sank into the mire right up to the axles.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'tire' — picture a tire spinning uselessly in thick mud.

words.definition: A confused, chaotic mass or jumble of many things.
words.example: A welter of clothes, books, and dishes buried the teenager's bedroom floor.
words.mnemonic: To 'welter' is to toss and roll like the sea — imagine waves heaving debris into one churning heap.

words.definition: A loud, confused noise made by an excited or agitated crowd.
words.example: The tumult of the packed stadium drowned out the referee's whistle.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'too-mult' — too many people all shouting at once.

words.definition: A state of noisy confusion or excited activity among people.
words.example: A sudden commotion at the back of the room made everyone spin around.
words.mnemonic: Break it as 'co + motion' — lots of motion together, bodies moving and shouting.

words.definition: Wild and noisy chaos, especially from a large, overexcited crowd.
words.example: When the winning goal went in, pandemonium erupted across the terraces.
words.mnemonic: In Milton's Paradise Lost it was the capital of Hell: 'pan' (all) + 'demon' — every demon in one place.

words.definition: A scene of noisy uproar and total confusion.
words.example: The classroom descended into bedlam the moment the teacher stepped out.
words.mnemonic: A nickname for Bethlem, London's notoriously chaotic old asylum.

words.definition: A powerful whirlpool, or a situation of violent, uncontrollable turbulence.
words.example: The sailors steered wide of the maelstrom churning between the jagged rocks.
words.mnemonic: From Dutch 'malen' (to grind) + 'stroom' (stream) — a stream that grinds you down.

words.definition: A whirling mass of water or air that pulls things toward its center.
words.example: The draining bathtub spun a tiny vortex right above the plughole.
words.mnemonic: Shares a root with 'vertex' and Latin 'vertere' (to turn) — it spins and turns.

words.definition: A state of untidiness or lack of organization.
words.example: Papers, mugs, and cables lay in complete disorder across his desk.
words.mnemonic: 'dis-' (not) glued to 'order' — literally 'not order'.

words.definition: An untidy collection of things scattered about in a messy way.
words.example: She could barely find her keys under the clutter on the hallway table.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'clot' + 'gutter' — stuff clotting up and jamming a gutter.

words.definition: Done without any clear plan, order, or method.
words.example: His haphazard packing meant he arrived with two left shoes and no socks.
words.mnemonic: 'hap' (luck, as in 'happen') + 'hazard' — left entirely to luck and chance.

words.definition: Not even or regular in pattern; unpredictable in movement or behavior.
words.example: The old car's erratic engine would surge and then stall without warning.
words.mnemonic: Shares a root with 'err' and 'error' — Latin 'errare', to wander off course.

words.definition: Likely to change suddenly and unexpectedly, often turning dangerous.
words.example: The crowd's mood grew volatile, cheering one minute and jeering the next.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'volare' (to fly) — it can take off or blow up any second.

words.definition: Changing loyalties, opinions, or affections often and without good reason.
words.example: Fickle fans adored the striker until his very first missed penalty.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'flicker' — a flame that flickers and shifts direction constantly.

words.definition: Unable to decide what to do; hesitant and lacking firmness.
words.example: Irresolute at the fork in the trail, he stood ten minutes and chose neither path.
words.mnemonic: 'ir-' (not) + 'resolute' — the exact opposite of firm and determined.

words.definition: Unable to make up one's mind or commit to a choice.
words.example: So indecisive over the menu, she finally let the waiter order for her.
words.mnemonic: 'in-' (not) + 'decisive' — pictures someone frozen, never able to pick.

words.definition: A statement that seems to contradict itself yet may still be true.
words.example: 'Less is more' is a paradox that designers love to quote.
words.mnemonic: Greek 'para-' (contrary to) + 'doxa' (opinion) — contrary to what you'd expect.

words.definition: Something that breaks from the normal pattern or expected rule.
words.example: Every sensor read a steady temperature except one, and engineers scrambled to explain the anomaly.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'a-NOT-a-many' — a NOT-normal thing standing apart from the many.

words.definition: A brief, unusual departure from what is typical or right.
words.example: Her rude outburst was such an aberration that friends assumed something serious was wrong.
words.mnemonic: 'Ab-' means away (as in absent); picture erring AWAY from your usual self.

words.definition: The act of moving apart or differing from a common point.
words.example: The two economists agreed at first, but a sharp divergence appeared once they discussed taxes.
words.mnemonic: 'Di-' = two, 'verge' = to turn — two paths turning away from each other.

words.definition: To turn aside from an established course, standard, or plan.
words.example: The pilot refused to deviate from the approved route even as passengers begged for a scenic detour.
words.mnemonic: 'De-' + 'via' (road) — to leave the road you were told to take.

words.definition: To confuse someone completely, leaving them unable to understand.
words.example: The magician's vanishing coin continued to mystify even the sharpest kids in the front row.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'mystery' — to wrap someone in a mystery they can't solve.

words.definition: To work out the meaning of something coded, faint, or hard to read.
words.example: It took her an hour to decipher the doctor's cramped scrawl on the prescription pad.
words.mnemonic: 'De-' (undo) + 'cipher' (a code) — undo the cipher to reveal the message.

words.definition: Expressed without clear order, so the parts do not connect or make sense.
words.example: Feverish and exhausted, he mumbled an incoherent string of words no one could follow.
words.mnemonic: 'In-' (not) + 'cohere' (stick together) — thoughts that won't stick together.
